Democrat Syed leads Republican Hills in one of the most expensive Illinois legislative races ever

Nabeela Syed outraised Darby Hills 2 to 1 in an Illinois Senate race that fetched $6.5 million in contributions.

On a night when Republicans were not expected to make much of a dent into Democrats’ supermajority in the Illinois General Assembly Tuesday, a pair of closely watched races were shaping up to be too close to call.

In one key race, state Rep. Nabeela Syed, a Democrat from Inverness, is challenging incumbent Republican Darby Hills of Barrington Hills for the Illinois Senate 26th District seat. With 23% of the votes counted, Syed led Hills with almost 58% of the vote.

The $6.5 million raised makes it one of the most expensive General Assembly contests ever, said Alisa Kaplan, executive director of Reform for Illinois.

Syed received at least $4.7 million in contributions, much of it from her party, while Hills has raised $1.8 million, said Kaplan, whose organization runs the Illinois Sunshine Database.

“The Democratic leadership wants to flip this seat, and it shows,” Kaplan said.

Syed raised more than $3 million from the Democratic Party of Illinois and the Illinois Senate Democratic Fund, controlled by Illinois Senate President Don Harmon. She’s also raised substantial amounts of money from unions.

Hills’ last big contribution from her party was in August when the Illinois Senate Republican Campaign gave her $300,000.

Separate from Hills’ own fundraising, a political action committee called the Strong Independent Leadership Committee formed last month to oppose Syed. It’s stated purpose is “ensuring only strong, independent leaders are elected by opposing extreme candidates,” according to a state filing.

Vince Foglia of North Barrington formed the political committee and contributed $500,000 to it.

Separately, Foglia and his family have also contributed $500,000 to Hills’ campaign.

The northwest suburban district includes parts of Cook, Lake, McHenry and Kane counties.

Hills was appointed to fill out the term of Dan McConchie, who resigned to take a job with a nonprofit organization.

Syed, 27, is completing her second term in the Illinois House , while Hills is completing the term of Dan McConchie, who resigned to take a job with a nonprofit organization. Syed was the youngest woman and one of the only Muslims ever to be elected to the Illinois General Assembly.

Hills, 50, has raised Syed’s youth and experience as a campaign issue. In the final days, she’s called Syed “too extreme” to represent her district.

“I’ve represented the community for four years,” Syed said in an interview. “I’m proud of my record. It’s disingenuous to call that extreme.”

Some Syed supporters took exception to the “too extreme” remark.

“It comes from a place of desperation,” Syed supporter Rija Arshad said Tuesday night. “There’s nothing else to hit Nabeela on because she’s strong on her issues.”

A former prosecutor and 2021 Mrs. Illinois America, Hills was a village trustee before being appointed to McConchie’s seat. She has campaigned for public safety, especially related to children, lower taxes and government spending controls.

Syed, a Palatine native, said affordability and access to healthcare are among her top priorities.

Both candidates call for more oversight of data center development, a contentious issue across the state.

Before Tuesday’s election, Democrats hold super-majorities in both the Illinois House (78-40) and Illinois Senate (40-19).

Elsewhere, Democrats were looking to unseat 52nd House District Republican Martin McLaughlin, who faced candidate Maria Peterson again.

With 24% of votes counted, Peterson led with 57% to 43% for McLaughlin.

In 2024, McLaughlin eked out a victory against Peterson, beating her by fewer than 50 votes.

Peterson cited affordability, environmental protection and safety atop the issues she was focusing on and pointed to her records as a lawyer doing advocacy work.

McLaughlin has said he’s focused on government spending and accountability.

And in Illinois Senate District 14, incumbent Democratic state Sen. Emil Jones III has been declared the winner, with 72.7% of the vote to 27.3% for Republican challenger Brian Skala, with about 58% of the vote in.

More than one-quarter of the members of the Illinois General Assembly represent Chicago or portions of the city, and the vast majority are Democrats.

Only one incumbent Democrat lost in March: State Rep. Jaime Andrade Jr. lost his primary for House District 40 to challenger and community activist Miguel Alvelo Rivera for the North Side seat. Rivera is unopposed in Tuesday’s election.

Republicans saw an opportunity in another rematch where Republican Liz Bishop was challenging incumbent Democrat Amy “Murri” Briel in the 76th Illinois House District race in north-central Illinois. The campaign includes some eyebrow-raising allegations.

However, Briel was leading with 66% after 19% of the votes were counted.

Democrat Josh Shapiro Wins Second Term as Pennsylvania Governor

Gov. Josh Shapiro (D-PA) won a second term as Pennsylvania's governor in Tuesday's midterm election. 
The post Democrat Josh Shapiro Wins Second Term as Pennsylvania Governor appeared first on Breitbart.

Actual Article Body:
Gov. Josh Shapiro (D-PA) won a second term as Pennsylvania’s governor in Tuesday’s midterm election.

The Associated Press called the race for Shapiro at shortly after 8:00 p.m. ET, just minutes after polls closed in the Keystone State. With 7 percent of the vote reported at 8:19 p.m. ET,  Shapiro led Republican gubernatorial nominee Stacy Garrity 80.8 percent to 18.4 percent, the New York Times’ election results show.

Shapiro led Garrity comfortably throughout October in the public polls available for the contest.

A Quinnipiac University poll of 1159 likely voters from October 1-5 found him up 25 points; a PennLive poll taken October 5-11 had him leading by 30 points; and an October 7-18 Franklin & Marshall poll showed him with a 23-point advantage—all safely outside the margins of error.

The governor had a substantial cash-on-hand advantage over Garrity in the month leading up to the election. In September, he had $19.8 million in cash on hand to Garrity’s $1.3 million, City and State Pennsylvania reported.

Garrity ran with President Donald Trump’s endorsement.

The president bashed Shapiro on Tuesday in a post on X reaffirming his support for Garrity. He called Shapiro “a Radical Left Dumocrat who wants massive Tax Increases, Open Borders, Men playing in Women’s Sports, and Transgender Mutilization of your Children.”

“Josh Shapiro is Reckless, Radical, and Dangerous!” he added.

The Democrat governor has not shied away from criticizing Trump, most recently on Sunday in an interview with CBS News’s Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan, where he accused the president of “cruelty” and “corruption.”

Shapiro, whose name was thrown out as a potential running mate for former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, is commonly speculated to be a potential presidential candidate for the Democratic nomination in 2028. During the interview, he dodged questions about a potential candidacy by focusing on the midterms.

Brennan pressed him on speculation from Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA) and Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE) that he could run in 2028.

“Well, and you’re welcome to ask. And look, I’m humbled that you would ask that question. I’m humbled by the responses the senator and the representative gave you. But the only thing I’m focused on is here in Pennsylvania, winning up and down the ballot,” he said.
